facts.fact_text: On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.

The aim of the demonstration was to protest against abuses and falsifications in the course of the elections to the State Duma and of the President of the Russian Federation, and to demand fair elections, respect for human rights, the rule of law and the international obligations of the Russian Federation.
The march proceeded down Yakimanka Street peacefully and without disruption.
On 6 May 2012 the applicant was arrested during the dispersal of a political rally at Bolotnaya Square in Moscow.
The applicant was detained at the police station for at least thirty-six hours pending administrative proceedings.

In the administrative proceedings, the applicant was found guilty of failure to obey lawful police orders, an offence under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
The applicant was sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.
Unlike on 4 February 2012, the park at Bolotnaya Square was excluded from the meeting venue on 6 May 2012, which was limited to Bolotnaya Embankment.

A cordon of riot police in full protection gear barred access to the park at Bolotnaya Square and continued along the whole perimeter of the meeting area, channelling the demonstration to Bolotnaya Embankment.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
The police applied combat techniques and used truncheons during the dispersal at 6.15 p.m.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.
The leaders of the march found that the layout of the meeting and the placement of the police cordon did not correspond to what they had anticipated.
Unlike on 4 February 2012, the park at Bolotnaya Square was excluded from the meeting venue on 6 May 2012, which was limited to Bolotnaya Embankment.

After the working meeting on 4 May 2012, the Moscow Department of the Interior prepared a security plan and map providing for the park at Bolotnaya Square to be cordoned off with metal barriers and for the participants in the meeting to be accommodated on the road at Bolotnaya Embankment.

The security plan and security maps were prepared at extremely short notice (during the night of 4-5 May 2012 and the day of 5 May 2012) and were approved on 5 May 2012 by senior officials at the Moscow Department of the Interior.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.

The Expert Commission noted that on 4 May 2012 the Moscow Department of the Interior published a plan on its website indicating that all of Bolotnaya Square, including the public gardens, would be given over to the rally, while Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge would be closed to vehicles but would remain open to pedestrians.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that when the march approached the venue of the meeting, they saw that the map showing where people would assemble on the square had been essentially altered, with the park at Bolotnaya Square, taking up approximately 80% of the square, barred and cordoned off.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the official website of the Moscow Department of the Interior published the map on which it was shown, just as agreed and just as on 4 February 2012, that the border of the meeting venue was outlined at the far end of the park and not the near one, and that all agreements were breached.
Mr B. Nemtsov testified that on the website of the Moscow Department of the Interior a map was posted showing that the park of Bolotnaya Square should have been open, but it turned out to be closed.
The 'reasons' section of the administrative detention order remained blank.

On the basis of the report written by Police Officer Y., the Justice of the Peace of circuit no. 100 of the Yakimanka district established that at 8.30 p.m. on 6 May 2012 the applicant had been walking along the road at Bolotnaya Square and obstructing the traffic, and that he had then disobeyed lawful police orders to vacate the venue.

The Zamoskvoretskiy District Court of Moscow rejected the applicant's argument that the police report and the police statement were inconsistent as regards the time of his arrest, finding that the correct interpretation was that the time of arrest had been 8.30 p.m. and the detention at the police station 9.30 p.m.

The security plan provided for security measures in Moscow city centre in view of the forthcoming authorised demonstration at Bolotnaya Square and anticipated attempts by other opposition groups to hold unauthorised public gatherings.

The security plan provided for an 8,094-strong crowd-control taskforce, comprising police and military, to police the designated security areas and to prevent unauthorised public gatherings and terrorist attacks.

According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, from 6 p.m. to 9 p.m. necessary measures were taken to push citizens away from Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, Bolotnaya Embankment and Bolotnaya Street and to arrest those who resisted the most, during which twenty-eight police officers and military servicemen sustained injuries of various gravity, four of whom were hospitalised.
According to Police Colonel D. Deynichenko's report, in total 656 people were detained in Moscow to prevent public disorder and unauthorised demonstrations.

According to the applicant, during the working meeting on 4 May 2012 the organisers and the authorities agreed that, since there was insufficient time for an on-the-spot reconnaissance, the assembly layout and the security arrangements would be identical to the previous public event organised by the same group of opposition activists on 4 February 2012.
On 4 February 2012, the previous public event had proceeded with a march down Yakimanka Street followed by a meeting at Bolotnaya Square.
The leaders of the march found that the layout of the meeting and the placement of the police cordon did not correspond to what they had anticipated.
Unlike on 4 February 2012, the park at Bolotnaya Square was excluded from the meeting venue on 6 May 2012, which was limited to Bolotnaya Embankment.
The cordon officers did not enter into any discussion with the protest leaders and no senior officer was delegated to negotiate.

During the period between 5.20 p.m. and 5.45 p.m., no senior police officers or municipal officials came to the site of the sit-down protest, and there was no direct communication between the authorities and the leaders of the sit-in.
At 6 p.m. Police Colonel A. Makhonin told Ms N. Mityushkina to make an announcement from the stage that the meeting was over.

Ms N. Mityushkina made the announcement from the stage that the meeting was over, but apparently her message was not heard by most of the demonstrators or the media reporters broadcasting from the spot.
The live television footage provided by the parties contained no mention of Ms N. Mityushkina's announcement that the meeting was over.
At 6.15 p.m., at the corner of Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, the riot police began breaking into the demonstration to split the crowd.
Running in tight formations, the riot police pushed the crowd apart, arrested some people, confronted others and formed new cordons to isolate sections of the crowd.
The police applied combat techniques and used truncheons during the dispersal at 6.15 p.m.
Through the loudspeakers the police requested that the participants leave for the metro station.
The dispersal of the demonstration continued for at least another hour until the venue was fully cleared of all protesters.

The security plan and security maps were prepared at extremely short notice (during the night of 4-5 May 2012 and the day of 5 May 2012) and were approved on 5 May 2012 by senior officials at the Moscow Department of the Interior.

The Moscow Department of the Interior did not discuss the security maps and security plan with the organisers, as those documents were for internal use showing the placement of the police forces and setting out their tasks.

The Expert Commission noted that the police did not inform the organisers of the changes they had decided upon, and the organisers only became aware of the police-imposed changes to the event when they arrived at the site on the afternoon of 6 May 2012.

The Expert Commission's report stated that as the march approached Bolotnaya Square, demonstrators found that a police cordon was blocking off most of the square, leaving only a narrow stretch along the waterfront for the rally.

The Expert Commission's report stated that from the moment difficulties first arose for demonstrators attempting to cross Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, demonstrators made repeated attempts to negotiate with the police over moving their cordons to allow protesters onto Bolotnaya Square.

The Expert Commission's report stated that Mr D. Oreshkin, a member of the Presidential Human Rights Council, and State Duma deputy Mr G. Gudkov tried to talk to the police authorities at around 5.30 p.m., but there was no response.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Ms N. Mityushkina as stating that she tried unsuccessfully to find the responsible people in the Ministry of the Interior to solve organisational problems, and that only at 6.00-6.30 p.m. did a senior police officer approach her and tell her that the authorities had suspended the demonstration and ask her to announce from the stage that the event was over.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Mr I. Bakirov as stating that a police officer in a colonel's uniform contacted him only once, and that later when clashes with the police erupted he could not find anyone with whom to communicate and cooperate.

The Expert Commission's report quoted organiser Mr S. Davidis as stating that he personally did not meet nor have time to get into contact with the authorities regarding the fences set up around the perimeter of the rally, and that he only saw OMON officers who behaved aggressively and were not predisposed to get into a conversation.

The Expert Commission's report stated that in the two hours between 6 p.m. and 8 p.m. there does not appear to have been any clear reason for the police decision to advance other than to divide the crowd up into smaller sections, and that there is little evidence that demonstrators initiated the violence.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at around 6.20 p.m. the police announced that the rally was cancelled and asked protesters to disperse, but the announcement was not loud enough to reach the majority of the crowd.

The Expert Commission's report stated that at the same time as the dispersal announcement, Police Colonel V. Biryukov, head of the Moscow Department of the Interior's press service, told a group of human rights defenders that the demonstrators could continue to Bolotnaya Square to take part in the rally.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that when the march approached the venue of the meeting, they saw that the map showing where people would assemble on the square had been essentially altered, with the park at Bolotnaya Square, taking up approximately 80% of the square, barred and cordoned off.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that since the cordon did not correspond to the map, the column stopped and the event organisers and the people who came just waited for the police to remove the wrong cordon and for the police chiefs to reply as to what had changed.

Mr A. Navalnyy testified that no authorities were present on the spot and it was impossible to understand who was in command, and that State Duma deputies present on the spot tried to act as negotiators but said that nobody wanted to come up to them.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the negotiations with the mayor's office were very difficult this time and that it was only on 4 May 2012 that the organisers received the written agreement, with practically twenty-four hours' notice.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the closure of the park was not discussed at the working meeting on 4 May 2012, and that it was expressly stated that everything except the position of the stage would be the same as on 4 February 2012.

Mr S. Davidis testified that the official website of the Moscow Department of the Interior published the map on which it was shown, just as agreed and just as on 4 February 2012, that the border of the meeting venue was outlined at the far end of the park and not the near one, and that all agreements were breached.
Mr S. Davidis testified that the police officers did not answer phone calls and he did not manage to find anyone in charge of the police.

Mr B. Nemtsov testified that on 4 February 2012 there was an authorised event where all of Bolotnaya Square was open with no cordons on Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, and they were sure that on 6 May 2012 it would be exactly the same, but the police had blocked Bolotnaya Square leaving a very narrow passage for the demonstrators.

Mr B. Nemtsov testified that they sat on the ground to show the police that they were not going to storm the Kremlin and Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge, and that State Duma deputy Mr G. Gudkov offered to be an intermediary in the negotiations between the protesters and the police but his attempts to negotiate came to nothing.

Ms N. Mirza testified that the second riot police cordon, which had stood between Bolshoy Kamennyy Bridge and Malyy Kamennyy Bridge, apparently approached the crowd, therefore the pressure built up from both sides.

Ms N. Mirza testified that as she was later told by Police Colonel V. Biryukov, the protesters had sat down on the ground because the passage had been narrowed down, and she confirmed that the passage was much narrower than usual and there were metal detectors which were not supposed to be there.

Mr N. Svanidze testified that on 6 May 2012 he was present as an observer and that when everybody headed towards the narrow bottleneck at the embankment it created a jam, several dozen people sat on the ground, and the cordon moved towards them.

Mr N. Svanidze testified that he asked why the passage would not be opened, but Police Colonel V. Biryukov kept turning his face away and would not answer, and Mr Svanidze understood that there was no point talking to him as he was not in command.
Mr N. Svanidze testified that neither the Ombudsman nor anyone else was able to get the passage widened despite requesting it.

Mr Vasilyev testified that the Ombudsman told Police Colonel V. Biryukov to let the cordon be moved back so that people could pass, but Police Colonel V. Biryukov told him that it was outside his powers and that he did not know in whose powers it was, at which point the police began breaking the crowd up.
According to the applicant, between 6 p.m. and 7 p.m. the area around him remained peaceful, although there was general confusion.
The applicant claimed that he had not heard any announcement of the termination of the meeting.

The applicant claimed that he had heard the police orders made through a megaphone to disperse, but in the general commotion he was unable to leave immediately and remained within the authorised meeting area until 7 p.m., when he was arbitrarily arrested by the police dispersing the demonstration.
The applicant denied that he had received any warning or orders before being arrested.
According to the applicant, there was no traffic at Bolotnaya Square at the time of his arrest; it was still suspended.
The 'reasons' section of the administrative detention order remained blank.
The applicant requested that the case be adjourned on the grounds that he was unfit to stand trial after the detention; this request was rejected in order to expedite the proceedings.
The applicant requested that the hearing be opened to the public; this request was rejected in order to expedite the proceedings.
The applicant requested that two police officers be examined as witnesses; this request was rejected in order to expedite the proceedings.
The Justice of the Peace rejected as unreliable two eyewitnesses' testimonies to the effect that the police had not given the applicant any orders or warnings before arresting him.
Ms S. testified that at 9.03 p.m. on 6 May 2012 she had been at Bolotnaya Square; the site had been fully cordoned off and the traffic had not resumed.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly adopted by the Venice Commission at its 83rd Plenary Session (Venice, 4 June 2010) provided that an assembly should be deemed peaceful if its organisers have professed peaceful intentions and the conduct of the assembly is non-violent, and that the term 'peaceful' should be interpreted to include conduct that may annoy or give offence, and even conduct that temporarily hinders, impedes or obstructs the activities of third parties.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that the policing of assemblies must be guided by the human rights principles of legality, necessity, proportionality and non-discrimination, and that the State has a positive duty to take reasonable and appropriate measures to enable peaceful assemblies to take place without participants fearing physical violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if a standoff or other dispute arises during the course of an assembly, negotiation or mediated dialogue may be an appropriate means of trying to reach an acceptable resolution.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that any prior restrictions should be formalised in writing and communicated to the organiser of the event within a reasonable timeframe, and that the relevant authorities must ensure that any restrictions imposed during an event are in full conformity with the law.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that no additional restrictions should be imposed by law enforcement personnel during an assembly unless absolutely necessary in light of demonstrably changed circumstances, and that the detention of participants during an assembly should meet a high threshold and should be used only in the most pressing situations when failure to detain would result in the commission of serious criminal offences.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement agencies should be proactive in engaging with assembly organizers, that there should be a nominated point of contact within the law enforcement agency whom protesters can contact before or during an assembly, and that the policing operation should be characterized by a policy of 'no surprises'.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that law enforcement officials should differentiate between peaceful and non-peaceful participants, and that neither isolated incidents of sporadic violence nor the violent acts of some participants are themselves sufficient grounds to impose sweeping restrictions on peaceful participants in an assembly.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that so long as assemblies remain peaceful, they should not be dispersed by law enforcement officials, and that dispersal of assemblies should be a measure of last resort.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that dispersal should not occur unless law enforcement officials have taken all reasonable measures to facilitate and protect the assembly from harm and unless there is an imminent threat of violence.

The Venice Commission Guidelines provided that if dispersal is deemed necessary, the assembly organiser and participants should be clearly and audibly informed prior to any intervention by law enforcement personnel, and participants should be given reasonable time to disperse voluntarily before law enforcement officials intervene further.
